topics.title: National income: boundaries, bridges and welfare
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Identify the production boundary, reconcile measurement approaches and distinguish output growth from welfare.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy's domestic territory during a period. 'Final' prevents counting the same production repeatedly. A good is not inherently final or intermediate: flour bought by a bakery is an input, whereas flour bought by a household for consumption is a final purchase. Production is measured for a period, so GDP is a flow rather than a stock of national wealth.

Domestic and national answer different questions. Domestic refers to where production occurs; national refers to income accruing to resident units. Residence is an economic concept, not a passport test. The income bridge is GNI = GDP + net primary/factor income from abroad, using compatible definitions and valuation. Gross measures include consumption of fixed capital; subtract it to obtain a corresponding net measure.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: The production method adds value created at successive stages. The income method adds income generated by production. The expenditure method measures final uses, commonly written C + I + G + (X - M). Imports are deducted because imported items may already appear in consumption, investment or government purchases; subtraction removes foreign production, not a judgement that imports have no benefit.

Nominal GDP values output at current prices; real GDP removes price changes through a volume measure. GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP x 100. GDP at market prices equals GVA at basic prices plus taxes on products minus subsidies on products. This bridge is not the same as adding every type of tax. GDP also differs from welfare: unpaid household services, distribution and environmental damage are not adequately described by the headline.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented production chain: a grower sells produce for 80, a processor sells its output for 150 and a retailer sells it for 190, with no other intermediate inputs. Value added is 80 + (150 - 80) + (190 - 150) = 190. Adding sales, 80 + 150 + 190 = 420, counts intermediate production again.

Invented price example: nominal output is 250 and real output is 200 in compatible units. The deflator is 125. That means the measured price level is 25% above its base, not that annual inflation is 125%. Annual change needs the previous year's comparable index. Reselling an old machine adds no new machine production, but a newly supplied brokerage service contributes current output.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not classify transfers as payment for newly produced services merely because money changes hands. Distinguish purchasing a newly issued financial claim from producing a physical capital asset. Financial transactions can finance investment without themselves being the investment measured in GDP.

Do not equate GVA and GDP, gross and net, citizenship and residence, or total GDP growth and per-capita improvement. The supplied notes have inconsistent GVA/base-year wording; these explanations use the conceptual distinctions without endorsing an unverified current series or release status.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For a question on GDP's limitations, first state what GDP measures well: the scale and growth of production. Then explain a missing dimension, such as distribution, unpaid care or environmental cost, and show why that changes welfare assessment. Conclude with complementary indicators rather than claiming GDP should be discarded. For a numerical question, write the boundary and valuation before selecting the formula.

topics.title: Growth and development: output, distribution and transformation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish real output expansion from inclusive development; explain productivity and structural change, then test jobs, capabilities and environmental costs rather than dumping GDP figures.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Economic growth means an increase in real output. Economic development is broader: it concerns improvements in living conditions, productive capabilities, institutions and opportunities. A growing economy has more resources with which to improve health and education, but the existence of resources does not tell us who receives them or whether public services actually work.

Per-capita output adjusts the aggregate for population, but remains an average. Development therefore asks additional questions: are people healthier and better educated, is poverty falling, are jobs productive, and are gains environmentally durable? Growth is an important enabling condition, not a sufficient measure of success in every one of these dimensions.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Output can expand by employing more labour and capital or by using them more productively. Investment adds capacity, while technology, skills, infrastructure and organisational improvements raise output obtainable from given inputs. Merely announcing an investment is insufficient: implementation and efficient use determine the productive gain.

Structural transformation means changes in the composition of production and employment. If workers move from low-productivity activities into better-paid productive jobs, incomes can rise. If a sector's output share rises without absorbing workers, transformation in GDP may coexist with insecure livelihoods. Inclusion is the transmission mechanism between expansion and improved lives, not an automatic consequence of a growth statistic.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented example: real output rises from 400 to 424, giving (424 - 400) / 400 x 100 = 6% growth. If population simultaneously rises by 3%, real output per person grows by 1.06 / 1.03 - 1, approximately 2.91%, not 6%. We still need distributional information before saying each household became better off.

A factory can increase output and create jobs while polluting the village's water. Its production gain belongs in the growth discussion; treatment costs, lost farm income and health damage belong in the welfare assessment. Development requires evaluating both sides, who bears each effect and what safeguards can change the outcome.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A rising average is not proof of falling inequality. A lower agricultural GDP share is not proof that agricultural workers have found better employment. A large spending allocation is an input, not a measured improvement in education or health.

Do not turn 'growth is not sufficient' into 'growth is unnecessary'. Equally, do not claim that growth will inevitably trickle down. State the channels: employment, earnings, public revenue, service delivery and social protection.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Build an answer as growth source -> transmission to households -> missing capability or distributional link -> corrective policy. For inclusive growth, connect productive employment and access to services rather than listing unrelated schemes. Finish with outcomes that would demonstrate success, such as earnings, learning or health improvements, alongside real per-capita growth.

topics.title: Human development: capabilities, human capital and feedback
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: explain real freedoms as the end of development, human capital as a productive means, the growth–capability feedback loop and why average index gains can hide exclusion.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Human development evaluates people's real opportunities to live lives they value. Income matters because it can buy useful goods and services, but income is a means rather than the whole objective. A person may have purchasing power yet be unable to obtain treatment, attend school safely or exercise meaningful choice.

Human capital treats health, skills and knowledge as productive capacities. The same education can be valuable both because it expands a person's freedom and because it increases productivity. The two perspectives overlap, but human development does not require every valuable activity to earn a financial return.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Health supports attendance, concentration and the ability to work. Education and training improve the ability to understand information, adopt technology and obtain productive employment. Higher incomes can then finance better health and learning, creating a reinforcing relationship. It is not automatic: poor-quality services, discrimination or a shortage of suitable jobs can interrupt it.

HDI combines health, education and income dimensions rather than using income alone. Its familiar components are life expectancy, education indicators and per-capita national income adjusted for purchasing power. Index construction aggregates dimensions; it does not describe every inequality, agency constraint or environmental problem. A headline rank also depends on other countries, so inspect the underlying dimension values.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative case: a household's income increases, but a daughter cannot attend secondary school because there is no safe transport and her unpaid care workload is high. Money has improved one resource without removing the binding constraints. A response combining accessible schooling, safe travel and care support addresses conversion of resources into actual opportunity.

Compare two districts with similar incomes. One has reliable primary healthcare and effective schools; the other has neither. The second district cannot be assumed equally developed from income alone. Ask which dimension is weak and which delivery bottleneck explains the gap instead of simply demanding more aggregate spending.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not substitute a human-capital argument for a complete human-development judgement: a person's worth is not their contribution to GDP. Do not equate school enrolment with learning or health expenditure with good health.

HDI, multidimensional poverty and an income-poverty measure answer different questions. Their scores and ranks are not interchangeable. An improvement in an index needs its edition, reference period and components before it can support a current claim.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: An analytical answer should identify a capability, the resource needed to support it, and the barrier preventing its use. Explain the two-way relationship with growth, then add a delivery or equity condition. Use health, education and income evidence together; do not make a rank substitute for the underlying explanation.

topics.title: Poverty: incidence, depth, capabilities and vulnerability
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish absolute, relative and multidimensional poverty; interpret incidence versus shortfall, trace poverty traps and match persistent deprivation or temporary shocks to suitable policy responses.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Poverty is deprivation relative to a stated standard. Monetary poverty uses an income or consumption threshold. Absolute poverty compares resources with a minimum standard, whereas relative poverty concerns disadvantage against the society's income distribution. Neither term is meaningful without specifying the benchmark and population.

Headcount incidence asks how many people are below the line. Depth asks how far below it they are. Severity gives greater weight to larger shortfalls. A policy can improve poor households' consumption without changing headcount if they remain below the threshold; dismissing that improvement would miss an important welfare gain.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Chronic poverty persists over time, often reflecting low assets, weak capabilities or exclusion. Transient poverty arises when a shock pushes a household into deprivation. The policy mix differs: durable livelihood and capability investment addresses persistent constraints; insurance, emergency support and portable benefits help absorb shocks.

Multidimensional poverty examines overlapping deprivations such as health, education and living standards. A household may cross a monetary line yet lack safe water or usable schooling. Conversely, an improvement in a public service need not immediately raise measured cash income. Treat these lenses as complementary and compare statistics only when their definitions and reference periods align.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented population of 100: 20 people consume 60 units each and the poverty line is 100. Headcount is 20%. Each poor person's normalised gap is 40%. The population poverty-gap index is (20 x 0.40) / 100 = 0.08, or 8%, assuming everyone else is above the line.

If these 20 people's consumption rises to 90, headcount remains 20% but the population gap falls to 2%. Squaring individual gaps would give extra weight to the initially larger shortfalls. These calculations are illustrations, not official poverty estimates or a claim that giving exactly the measured gap is administratively sufficient to eliminate poverty.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: An individual poverty gap is not the population poverty-gap index. A decline in poverty does not establish that inequality declined. A poverty line is not the same thing as average income or an eligibility rule for every welfare scheme.

Do not compare a monetary poverty percentage with a multidimensional percentage as if they were rival measurements of an identical quantity. Identify survey/reference year, population, threshold and method first. Beneficiary counts are not automatically counts of people lifted out of poverty.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Explain the cause before prescribing the intervention: low earnings, weak capabilities, exclusion or exposure to shocks. Link jobs and productivity to durable income gains, public services to capability gains, and protection to resilience. Evaluate incidence and depth together and mention targeting, access and delivery rather than presenting a scheme list as proof of impact.

topics.title: Employment: people, participation and measurement
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate the labour force, workers and unemployed before interpreting a rate. This pilot covers selected concepts, not the entire unemployment chapter.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: The labour force contains employed people and unemployed people who meet the survey's job-search and availability criteria. The workforce contains employed people only. People outside the labour force are not automatically unemployed: they may be studying, performing unpaid household duties or not seeking/available for work under the relevant definition.

LFPR = labour force / population of the specified group x 100. WPR = employed / population of that same group x 100. Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force x 100. All three require an age group, reference period and activity-status definition. Without those, a percentage is incomplete.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Employment and unemployment change through both job outcomes and participation. Someone finding work moves from unemployed to employed. Someone stopping job search may move out of the labour force. Both can reduce measured unemployment, but their economic meaning is very different.

Employment quality matters beyond the employed/not-employed distinction. Hours, productivity, earnings, security and access to protection affect livelihoods. Seasonal unemployment concerns work availability at different times of year; disguised underemployment concerns workers whose removal would not materially reduce output in the stylised example. Structural mismatch differs from a cyclical fall in demand.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented group: population 1,000, labour force 600, employed 540. Unemployed people number 60. LFPR is 60%, WPR is 54%, and unemployment is 60 / 600 x 100 = 10%. Dividing the unemployed by total population would produce 6%, which is not the unemployment rate.

Now suppose 20 unemployed people stop searching and leave the labour force; employment remains 540. The labour force becomes 580 and unemployment becomes 40 / 580 = 6.90%. The unemployment rate fell without a single new job. Read LFPR and WPR together before calling this an improvement in labour demand.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A lower unemployment rate is not unconditionally good news. Higher LFPR may initially raise measured unemployment if new entrants seek jobs faster than employers create them. Neither a survey headline nor registration on a jobs portal proves all workers have secure, adequately paid work.
Do not mix usual-status and short-reference-period estimates, rural and urban groups, or different ages. A comparison can be numerically correct but economically invalid if its populations differ.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For an employment answer, separate labour supply, job creation and job quality. Connect skills and care constraints to participation, investment and demand to opportunities, and worker protection to quality. Use a matched LFPR/WPR/unemployment set, then explain the policy trade-off rather than inferring success from one rate.

topics.title: Sustainability: resource limits, policy and intergenerational equity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: connect present needs with future resource availability, explain growth–environment mechanisms, evaluate policy instruments and SDG implementation without treating an income threshold as automatic environmental repair.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Sustainable development asks how present needs can be met without undermining future generations' ability to meet theirs. It combines economic opportunity, social inclusion and environmental integrity. The point is not to stop all resource use, but to account for regeneration, depletion, damage and access over time.

A renewable resource can replenish, but extraction may still exceed its replenishment. An exhaustible resource cannot simply be regenerated on the relevant timescale. Sustainability therefore depends on the rate and method of use, ecosystem resilience and the availability of substitutes, not merely the renewable/non-renewable label.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Pollution is a negative externality when some costs fall on people outside the transaction. Private decisions may then generate too much pollution relative to a social-cost benchmark. Standards constrain harmful activity, pricing can change incentives, and public investment can make cleaner alternatives feasible. Enforcement and distribution matter: a charge without practical alternatives may disproportionately burden vulnerable users.

Efficiency means fewer inputs or emissions per unit of output. Total environmental pressure may still rise if production expands sufficiently. The environmental Kuznets curve describes a possible inverted-U relationship between income and some pollutants; it is not a law guaranteeing automatic clean-up. Technology, policy and institutions help determine the path.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented forest: annual regeneration is 8 units and harvest is 11. The stock faces a 3-unit annual depletion pressure, ignoring other changes. Calling the forest renewable does not make that harvest sustainable. A plan must address extraction, regeneration and ecological thresholds, not only plant trees elsewhere.

Suppose emissions per unit fall from 10 to 8, but output rises from 100 to 150. Total emissions rise from 1,000 to 1,200. Efficiency improved by 20% while total pressure increased by 20%. The example shows why intensity and absolute outcomes must both be assessed.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate a climate pledge, conference theme or published strategy with achieved emission reduction. GDP growth does not deduct every environmental cost. Environmental accounts improve information but do not by themselves change behaviour.

SDGs form a linked agenda, not independent boxes. An energy project may affect jobs, health, water and ecosystems simultaneously. Index ranks depend on the chosen indicators, weights and comparison group; inspect them before declaring broad success.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Use the chain economic activity -> environmental/social pressure -> incentive or institutional failure -> policy mix -> measurable outcome. Include transition costs and vulnerable groups. A balanced answer explains both why growth is needed and what makes its resource use and distribution sustainable.

topics.title: Demography: population change, dependency and the dividend
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: separate natural increase from migration, interpret crude rates and age composition, and explain why a demographic opportunity produces growth only with health, skills, participation and productive jobs.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Demography studies population size, composition and change. Population changes through births, deaths and net migration. Natural increase is births minus deaths; actual change adds net migration. Age structure matters because children, working-age adults and older people have different service and livelihood needs.

Crude birth and death rates usually express births or deaths per 1,000 mid-year population. They are called crude because they do not adjust for the population's age structure. A total population change therefore cannot be read as a fertility change, and a high crude death rate does not by itself establish poor health services.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: In the stylised demographic transition, mortality may fall before fertility, widening the gap between births and deaths and accelerating population growth. Fertility may subsequently decline as education, child survival, urbanisation and household choices change. Stage numbering differs across descriptions; the underlying sequence is more useful than memorising disputed labels.

A larger working-age share creates a potential demographic dividend by lowering age dependency and enlarging productive capacity. Realisation needs health, skills, participation and enough productive jobs. A working-age person is not necessarily working. Later ageing creates needs for income security, healthcare and care services, making long-term planning necessary.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented year: births 900, deaths 400, arrivals 250 and departures 100, with mid-year population 50,000. Natural increase is 500 and total increase is 650. Birth rate is 18 per thousand and death rate is 8 per thousand. Their 10-per-thousand difference describes natural increase, excluding migration.

For age dependency, suppose a defined working-age group numbers 600 and the dependent-age groups together number 400. The age-dependency ratio is 400 / 600 x 100 = 66.7 per 100 working-age people. This is not a count of actual workers supporting actual non-workers; the group boundaries and employment status differ.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A favourable age mix is an opportunity, not a guaranteed growth outcome. Crude rates should not be used to rank health systems without examining age composition. A sex ratio must identify whether it concerns births or the entire population and state the convention used.

Population projections are conditional on fertility, mortality and migration assumptions. Never treat a future projection as an observed count. Distinguish a census, a sample survey, an estimate and a projection.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Organise a demographic-dividend answer around opportunity -> capability -> participation -> productive employment -> preparedness for ageing. Link women's work, health and education to realisation of the potential. Explain the mechanism and use dated population evidence rather than treating population size itself as either a burden or a dividend.

topics.title: Health: prevention, access and financial protection
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: explain health as well-being and a development input, distinguish prevention from treatment and financial protection from service availability, and prepare one coherent delivery-reform answer.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Health is more than the absence of a diagnosed disease: physical, mental and social functioning affect the ability to learn, work and participate. A health system must prevent avoidable illness, provide timely quality treatment and protect households from unaffordable expenditure.

Financial access and physical availability are separate. Insurance or public financing can reduce the price paid at the point of care, but cannot by itself create a nearby clinician, functioning laboratory or reliable medicines. Effective coverage means a person can obtain appropriate care of adequate quality when needed, not merely hold a card.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Poor health can reduce workdays, productivity and school attendance while increasing treatment costs. These effects can push a vulnerable household into debt and poverty. Prevention, nutrition, sanitation and early care can interrupt this chain before expensive treatment becomes necessary.

Public-health interventions often generate benefits beyond the individual user. A hospital-centred strategy alone can neglect prevention and primary care. Public and private providers may both contribute, but ownership is not a substitute for assessing quality, affordability, accountability and access for underserved groups.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative case: a rural family has hospital coverage but the nearest qualified provider is far away and transport is unreliable. The benefit removes one financing barrier but leaves the supply and access constraints. Strengthening local primary care, referrals, medicine availability and transport complements financial protection.

Suppose a programme reports more people screened. That is an activity measure. To assess impact, follow the chain: screening -> correct diagnosis -> affordable treatment -> adherence -> better health. Losses at any step can prevent the initial activity from improving outcomes. No numerical benefit multiplier is assumed here.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Spending, insurance enrolment and facility construction are inputs or intermediate outputs, not the same as healthier lives. Averages may conceal rural, gender and income inequalities. A reported indicator needs its survey population and reference period.

Avoid a false choice between prevention and cure, or a claim that private/public ownership always determines performance. Unverified survey timing in supplied compilations should not be presented as a settled latest estimate.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For a health answer, combine prevention, service capacity, financial protection and accountability. Explain how each addresses a different bottleneck. Use an outcome such as avoidable illness or financial hardship alongside access measures, and connect health to human development without reducing its value solely to productivity.

topics.title: Education: access, learning and equitable opportunity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: distinguish forms of learning, enrolment and meaningful educational opportunity; explain access–quality–equity and prepare a reform answer that separates policy aspirations from achieved results.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Education builds knowledge, skills and the ability to make informed choices. It is both a development objective and an investment in productive capability. Access, continuation, learning and transition to further study or work are separate stages; success at one stage does not establish success at all.

Formal education is structured within recognised institutions. Non-formal education is organised learning outside the conventional system. Informal learning arises through daily experience without necessarily following an organised programme. These routes can complement each other, especially for learners excluded from ordinary provision.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: More places and lower costs can raise enrolment. Learning also depends on teaching quality, attendance, language accessibility, materials and an appropriate learning environment. Nutrition, health and household care burdens influence whether a learner can use the opportunity. Skills translate into earnings only when suitable work and fair access exist.

Gross enrolment ratio compares total enrolment at a level, irrespective of learners' ages, with the population in that level's official age group. It measures participation, not mastery. Retention and completion reveal different losses; assessment of learning is needed to evaluate acquired competencies.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented level: 1,080 people are enrolled and the official age-group population is 1,000. GER is 108%. This is possible because some enrolled learners are younger or older than the official range. It does not show that every age-eligible child is enrolled, nor that all those enrolled can read or perform the required tasks.

A district builds classrooms and raises enrolment, yet many children leave before completion. Investigate attendance, learning support, safety, household costs and the move to the next level. The right response preserves expanded access while addressing the stage where learners are being lost.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: GER is not a literacy rate, completion rate or learning score. A legal right and a policy announcement require actual delivery; targets should never be written as achieved outcomes. A higher allocation does not prove that funds were used effectively.

Do not assume education alone removes joblessness or gender barriers. It improves capability, while labour demand, discrimination, care responsibilities and infrastructure affect conversion into opportunity.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Structure an education answer as access -> retention -> learning -> equitable transitions. Diagnose the weak stage and match a measure to its cause. Explain complementarities with health, nutrition and livelihoods. Use policy directions as intentions unless implementation and outcome evidence have been established.

topics.title: Gender: agency, resources, care and participation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: use health, education, work and representation as distinct lenses; explain how norms, unpaid care and asset control shape agency, then evaluate an equity-oriented policy mix without relying on one headline ratio.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Gender analysis examines how social roles, institutions and power shape opportunities. Equality of legal entitlement is important, but people may still differ in actual access to education, work, property, safety and decision-making. Agency means the ability to make and act on meaningful choices, not merely receive a benefit.

Equality and equity are related but distinct. An identical rule provides formal equality; support responsive to unequal starting conditions can improve substantive opportunity. Women are not a homogeneous group: income, location, disability and other disadvantages can change the barriers faced.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Unequal unpaid care work limits time for education and paid employment. Safety constraints and inaccessible transport narrow the set of feasible jobs. Weak property rights or practical control can constrain borrowing and bargaining power. Education helps, but does not automatically remove these constraints.

LFPR measures labour-force participation, including eligible job seekers; WPR measures employment. Representation measures presence in institutions, while substantive voice asks whether people influence decisions. Sex ratio describes population composition, not the extent of agency or freedom within households.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative case: a qualified woman cannot accept a distant job because childcare is unavailable and travel is unsafe. The constraint is not simply a skill deficit. Reliable care services, safe transport and fair workplace access act on the missing links between capability and employment.

Invented birth counts of 30,000 girls and 32,000 boys give 30,000 / 32,000 x 1,000 = 937.5 girls per 1,000 boys under the Indian convention. This is the sex ratio at birth, not the overall population sex ratio. Neither measure alone tells us who owns assets or controls household decisions.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate a seat, bank account or legal title with effective control. A rise in participation can coexist with poor-quality work, and an income transfer is not by itself proof of empowerment.

Legal proposals, enacted provisions, notified rules and effective implementation are different stages. Supplied source-era legal claims need verification; these notes do not endorse an unverified legal change or a universal beneficiary rule.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For an empowerment answer, connect resources, agency and outcomes. Explain how a specific barrier restricts choice and how a measure changes it. Combine representation with voice, education with job access, and financial inclusion with actual control. Evaluate who is reached and who remains excluded rather than listing programmes as automatic successes.

topics.title: Positive discrimination: substantive equality and representation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: explain why identical treatment can preserve historical disadvantage, distinguish reservation from wider inclusion and evaluate representation, targeting and complementary capability support without asserting unverified legal details.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Positive discrimination or affirmative action provides targeted support to address accumulated disadvantage and exclusion. The central distinction is between formal equality, applying an identical rule, and substantive equality, making opportunity meaningfully accessible despite unequal starting conditions.

Reservation is one instrument, not the entire inclusion agenda. Scholarships, preparation, accessible institutions, protection from discrimination and support after entry address different constraints. The rationale and design must be distinguished from an assertion that every beneficiary has the same need.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Historical exclusion can reduce schooling, networks, assets and representation across generations. Identical entry rules may then reproduce unequal opportunity. Targeted entry support can open an institutional door, but the gains depend on continued learning, fair treatment, completion and progression.

There can also be unequal benefit capture within eligible groups. Appropriate targeting and review require category-specific law and evidence rather than a single assumed income test. Representation and social mobility are related outcomes, but a count of admitted students does not establish either learning quality or later advancement.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative university: access increases for previously excluded learners, but many entrants lack foundational preparation and leave early. The admission measure has improved entry; the next bottleneck is continuation. Academic support, accessible facilities and protection from discrimination complement admission rather than negate its rationale.

Compare two evaluation measures: the share of places filled and the share of entrants who complete and progress. The first is a delivery/output indicator; the second moves closer to sustained opportunity. Both are useful, but they answer different questions.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not claim all differential treatment is inherently unfair or that every targeted measure automatically solves exclusion. Eligibility, educational access, employment and political representation are different legal and institutional contexts.

Avoid presenting outdated percentages, proposed legal changes or a simplified 'creamy layer' rule as universally applicable. Exact current category rules need separate legal verification. The conceptual explanation does not establish a rule for a particular applicant.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Build the answer around the initial disadvantage, the intervention's mechanism, the opportunity created and the remaining barrier. Evaluate representation and mobility alongside implementation. A balanced conclusion can support effective inclusion while explaining the need for complementary services, accurate targeting and evidence-based review.

topics.title: Multiculturalism: recognition, inclusion and common citizenship
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: distinguish the fact of cultural diversity from policies of accommodation, compare recognition with redistribution and balance group protection with individual rights and shared civic participation.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Cultural diversity describes the existence of different languages, beliefs and ways of life. Multiculturalism concerns how institutions recognise and accommodate those differences while supporting equal citizenship. A place can be diverse but still organise services and participation in ways that exclude minorities.

Recognition addresses dignity, identity and meaningful participation. Redistribution addresses material resources and opportunity. Disadvantage can involve both: a household may need income support and also face exclusion because its language or identity is not accommodated.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Assimilation asks people to conform to dominant norms; accommodation makes reasonable room for difference. The policy problem is to enable shared civic participation without unnecessarily requiring cultural erasure. Common services can be designed to improve accessibility while protecting equal rights.

Group protection also requires attention to individuals within groups. A claim made in the name of a community may not reflect every member's interests. Evaluate both majority-minority relations and the freedom of women, dissenters and vulnerable members within a community. Recognition is not a blanket exemption from individual rights.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative city: a cultural festival celebrates a minority community, but residents cannot understand essential service information because it is available only in the majority language. Symbolic recognition has increased without solving access. Suitable language support and channels for participation address the practical barrier.

A cash transfer may improve the household's resources while leaving discriminatory treatment unchanged. Conversely, recognition without usable education, healthcare or employment can remain symbolic. The two policy dimensions complement one another.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate diversity with inclusion, cultural celebration with equal opportunity, or community representation with consent from every community member. Migration status, culture and legal citizenship are not interchangeable categories.

Avoid treating accommodation and common citizenship as automatically incompatible. The relevant questions are what barrier exists, what adjustment is proportionate and whether equal rights remain protected.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: A strong answer moves from recognition to access and participation. Explain a specific exclusion mechanism, combine cultural accommodation with material opportunity where relevant, and include individual rights as a safeguard. Assess outcomes in public-service use, voice and fair opportunity rather than counting festivals or declarations.

topics.title: Urbanisation and migration: drivers, agglomeration and inclusion
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish urban population growth from migration alone, explain push–pull drivers and agglomeration, assess origin/destination effects and match urban-service and inclusion policies to real constraints.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Urban growth is an increase in the number of urban residents. Urbanisation is an increase in the urban share of the total population. Urban population changes through natural increase, migration and reclassification or boundary changes, so not every additional resident is a rural migrant.

Migration involves movement across a specified boundary and period. It may be internal or international, temporary or long-term, voluntary or constrained by displacement. Origin-side push factors and destination-side pull factors can operate together; a single story rarely explains every movement.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Cities can raise productivity through agglomeration: workers and firms gain access to larger markets, suppliers, information and specialised skills. Those benefits depend on functioning housing, transport and services. Congestion, insecure housing and exclusion can raise costs and prevent residents from sharing the gains.

Migrants may contribute to production while struggling to access housing or portable benefits. Urban policy should connect livelihoods with basic services rather than view migration only as a burden. International mobility arrangements concern different institutions and permissions from ordinary rural-urban movement.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented city: urban population increases by 20,000; births minus deaths contribute 8,000 and reclassification contributes 5,000. With consistent boundaries and no other components, residual net migration is 20,000 - 8,000 - 5,000 = 7,000. Equating the entire increase with migration would overstate it.

If a city's urban population grows from 100 to 110 while the relevant total population grows from 200 to 230, urban numbers rose but the urban share fell from 50% to about 47.8%. Urban growth occurred without urbanisation under the share definition.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not call every migrant a refugee, every move voluntary or every rise in urban numbers urbanisation. State the boundary, population base and time period before comparing movement statistics.

A conference theme, smart-city platform or transport award does not prove better access. Evaluate travel time, affordability, safety and usable links to jobs and services, including for low-income residents.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Frame the answer as drivers -> agglomeration opportunities -> service/congestion constraints -> inclusive planning. Connect transport and housing to productive work, and portability to migrant access. Use definitions and components before presenting a migration or urban-population statistic.

topics.title: Inflation: measurement, causes and limits of policy
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Identify the relevant price measure and shock before explaining monetary transmission and the growth-price trade-off.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, not simply a rise in one commodity's price. An index combines prices with specified weights. Because consumers and producers buy different baskets at different stages, CPI and WPI can move differently without either calculation necessarily being wrong.

Disinflation means a reduction in the inflation rate: prices can still be rising. Deflation means a falling general price level. Headline inflation uses the full specified basket; core measures exclude defined components. There is no valid shortcut of subtracting a food-inflation percentage from headline inflation without considering weights and construction.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Demand-pull pressure arises when spending grows faster than available supply; cost-push pressure arises from higher costs or supply disruption. Imported inflation can arise through higher foreign prices or a weaker domestic currency raising domestic costs. Pass-through depends on pricing, taxes, competition and other conditions.

Tighter monetary policy can restrain demand, borrowing and expectations, but cannot directly create a missing crop or transport fuel. Supply measures address availability and logistics. An appropriate response depends on the shock and the risk that temporary price pressure spreads. Stagflation exposes the difficulty of weak output alongside inflation.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented fixed basket: base-period cost 800, last-year cost 960 and current cost 1,008. Last year's index is 120; the current index is 126. Annual inflation is (126 - 120) / 120 x 100 = 5%. The 26% increase from the base is not the current annual inflation rate.

If inflation falls from 8% to 5%, an item following the general price level still becomes more expensive, just more slowly. Also, a high previous comparison base can lower a year-on-year inflation rate without a current price fall. Check index levels as well as percentage changes.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not treat every supply shock as excess demand or claim rate increases have no role whenever food prices rise. Explain direct supply limits and indirect demand/expectation channels separately.

Avoid mixing an index level with an inflation rate, year-on-year with month-on-month movement, or a current rate with an unverified target/band. A central-bank objective and an observed inflation number are different types of information.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Use diagnosis -> transmission -> response -> limitation. Identify demand, cost or imported channels; explain who is affected, particularly households with little capacity to absorb price increases. Combine monetary and supply-side measures as appropriate, and specify the index and period for any numerical claim.

topics.title: Banks and RBI: development, inclusion and policy transmission
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate financial intermediation from central-bank policy and evaluate whether formal access becomes usable, resilient finance.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Banks connect savers with borrowers and provide payment services. A bank deposit is a liability of the bank; a loan made by the bank is an asset. Intermediation supports households and investment, but mismatches in maturity, credit quality and liquidity create risks that require sound management and regulation.

RBI's roles include monetary policy, currency issuance, banking regulation/supervision, management of relevant reserves and banking services to government. Do not confuse these functions with the commercial lending decisions of individual banks or with the mandates of other financial regulators.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: A policy-rate change influences market rates, banks' funding costs and ultimately borrowing conditions. Credit demand, bank balance sheets, competition and expectations affect how strongly it is transmitted. A change at the policy end therefore need not produce an equal, immediate change in every lending rate.

Liquidity is the ability to meet payments when due; solvency concerns whether assets can cover liabilities. A sound borrower can face a temporary cash-flow problem, while repeated liquidity support does not repair fundamentally bad assets. Financial inclusion also goes beyond opening an account: usage, suitability, affordability and protection determine whether access improves resilience.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative small firm: orders improve, but the firm cannot obtain working capital because its records are weak and the bank cannot assess repayment. A lower policy rate helps funding costs but may not remove that information barrier. Better records, risk assessment and an appropriate product address the missing link.

Suppose many depositors request cash at once. Even a bank with valuable longer-term loans may face immediate liquidity pressure because those assets cannot instantly be turned into cash without loss. This explains the importance of liquidity management; it does not establish that the bank is insolvent.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A loan is not a gift; a guarantee is not the same as a loan or subsidy. Opening accounts is not evidence that all intended users save, transact or obtain affordable credit. A regulatory recommendation is not automatically an operative rule.

Do not memorise stale cash-reserve ratios, policy rates, bank counts or eligibility thresholds as permanent concepts. When facts are date-sensitive, retain issuer, scope and effective date alongside the value.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For inclusion or transmission, explain the chain and locate the blockage: access, information, funding, risk appetite, demand or protection. Connect digital reach with usability and fraud safeguards. For RBI questions, identify the role and tool before describing the expected effect and its limits.

topics.title: Fiscal policy: deficits, stabilisation and consolidation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Link the budget's allocation, redistribution and stabilisation roles to deficit measures, financing choices and policy trade-offs.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Fiscal policy is the use of government taxation, expenditure and financing to influence activity, distribution and development. Expansionary policy supports demand through higher spending or lower taxes; contractionary policy restrains it. The effect depends on spare capacity, spending composition, financing and how households and firms respond.

Fiscal deficit = total expenditure - revenue receipts - non-debt capital receipts. It expresses a financing requirement under the stated accounting framework. Borrowing is not deducted as a receipt in this calculation: doing so would hide the borrowing requirement we are trying to measure.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure - revenue receipts. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - the specified interest payments. Effective revenue deficit deducts grants for creation of capital assets from revenue deficit. These measures answer different questions: the overall financing gap, the revenue-account gap and the part excluding inherited interest costs.

Automatic stabilisers respond without a fresh discretionary decision, for example tax collections weakening during a downturn. Discretionary measures require a policy change. Consolidation seeks sustainable public finances, but its timing and composition matter: cutting useful services or investment during weak demand can have very different consequences from reducing waste.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented budget, same units: total expenditure 500, revenue expenditure 350, revenue receipts 300, non-debt capital receipts 20, interest payments 40 and asset-creation grants 15. Fiscal deficit is 180; revenue deficit 50; primary deficit 140; effective revenue deficit 35.

If government borrows the 180 financing gap, that borrowing does not turn the fiscal deficit into zero. Borrowing finances it. Likewise, a grant intended to create an asset can be revenue expenditure in the grantor's accounts; its purpose and accounting classification need not be identical.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A deficit is not automatically money printing, inflation or waste. Spending may activate idle capacity or improve future supply; it may also add price, interest or debt-servicing pressure when resources are constrained.

Primary balance is not the same as overall balance, and a revenue-account label is not a complete measure of developmental value. Teacher salaries can support human capital even though their accounting treatment is revenue expenditure.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: State the objective and macro context, choose the spending/tax channel, explain financing and evaluate the trade-off. In a downturn, discuss demand and protection; for consolidation, discuss revenue quality and spending composition. Use deficit measures as analytical tools, not as interchangeable labels for good or bad governance.

topics.title: Public expenditure and receipts: classify before evaluating
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate accounting classification, economic purpose and financing consequences when assessing public finances.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Government accounting separates revenue and capital transactions. The distinction is about the nature of the asset or liability change, not simply whether a payment is large, useful or made only once. Revenue expenditure generally covers operations and transfers; direct acquisition of an asset or repayment of a liability is capital in character.

Revenue receipts include tax revenue and non-tax revenue such as interest and dividends. Capital receipts include borrowing, which creates a liability, and receipts such as loan recoveries or disinvestment, which reduce assets. Selling an asset can finance expenditure without creating debt, but is not a repeatable operating-income stream.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: A transfer provides income without purchasing a current good or service from the recipient. The recipient may subsequently buy goods, but that is a separate transaction. This distinction prevents treating every government money payment as production.

Spending quality cuts across accounting classes. Maintaining an asset can be crucial even though maintenance is revenue expenditure. An unproductive capital project can create an asset on paper without adequate public benefit. Grants for asset creation also require care: the grantor's revenue expenditure and the recipient's eventual capital formation are distinct entries.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative government buys a machine, pays for routine servicing and pays interest on the borrowing used to acquire it. Direct purchase creates an asset; servicing and interest are revenue expenditure. Repayment of the loan principal reduces a liability and differs from interest.

A dividend received is non-tax revenue. Recovery of a previously advanced loan is a non-debt capital receipt. Issuing a new bond is a debt-creating capital receipt. These can all provide cash today while having very different implications for future assets, liabilities and recurring fiscal capacity.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Recurring versus one-off is only a clue, not the decisive test. Developmental/non-developmental labels used in older discussions are not the revenue/capital distinction. Spending less on maintenance is not necessarily fiscal efficiency.

The supplied expenditure notes and fiscal notes conflict on grants for assets. These explanations preserve the grantor-versus-recipient distinction rather than teaching that every asset-related grant is direct capital expenditure.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For classification questions, ask who records the transaction, what is acquired or extinguished and whether a liability is created. For evaluative questions, separately assess purpose, delivery and outcomes. An answer is stronger when it distinguishes good accounting classification from good spending quality.

topics.title: Public debt: financing, risk and sustainability
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Evaluate debt using its use, servicing burden, maturity and currency risk rather than a single headline ratio.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Public debt is a stock of outstanding government liabilities at a date. A fiscal deficit is a financing gap over a period. Debt can increase because deficits accumulate, but valuation and other stock-flow adjustments also matter. Always state whether a statistic covers the Union, states or combined government.

Debt sustainability means the government can service obligations without implausible adjustment or loss of stability. The debt/GDP ratio helps compare liabilities with the economy's income-generating scale, but maturity, interest costs, revenue capacity and currency exposure also influence risk.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Short maturities can concentrate refinancing needs: old debt must be repaid or replaced quickly. Longer maturities spread rollover risk but do not erase interest costs. Refunding replaces maturing obligations; debt retirement actually extinguishes them. A lower interest burden after refinancing is possible, not guaranteed.

Creditor residence and contractual currency are separate dimensions. External exposure requires attention to exchange-rate and financing conditions, while domestic borrowing can affect local interest rates and private access to funds. Debt used for effective infrastructure may increase future capacity; inefficient spending leaves servicing obligations without comparable returns.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented figures: debt 600, GDP 1,000, annual interest 36 and revenue receipts 180. Debt/GDP is 60%; interest/revenue is 20%. If debt rises to 630 while GDP rises to 1,100, debt/GDP falls to about 57.27%. A falling ratio does not mean the nominal debt stock fell.

Replacing a maturing 100-unit bond with a new 100-unit bond meets today's repayment need but leaves the principal outstanding. Evaluate the new maturity and interest terms before calling it a debt reduction. These invented values imply no universal safe-debt threshold.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: National external debt includes obligations beyond government; it is not automatically sovereign external debt. A stock is not a deficit flow. A primary surplus can help debt dynamics without immediately eliminating all borrowing or accumulated debt.
Do not infer safety from a single ratio or claim every borrowing-funded project crowds out private investment. Capacity conditions and project quality can also produce crowding-in effects.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: A debt answer should examine size, cost, maturity, currency and purpose, then revenue capacity and growth. Discuss credible fiscal adjustment and spending quality instead of an unsupported universal ceiling. Distinguish temporary refinancing relief from a durable improvement in servicing capacity.

topics.title: Federal finance: powers, sharing and intergovernmental support
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Distinguish tax assignment, tax sharing, grants and borrowing constraints within India's fiscal federation.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Fiscal federalism allocates revenue powers and spending responsibilities across government tiers. A vertical imbalance arises when a tier's assigned revenues do not match its responsibilities. Horizontal imbalance refers to differences in capacity and needs across jurisdictions at the same tier.

Levying a tax, collecting it and retaining its proceeds are distinct functions. The fact that the Union collects a tax does not mean it retains every rupee. Tax devolution shares eligible proceeds; grants provide another transfer channel, sometimes linked to particular purposes or conditions.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Vertical distribution asks how resources are divided between the Union and states. Horizontal distribution asks how the states' share is divided among states. Population, need, fiscal capacity and incentives involve different considerations; an answer should identify which allocation question it is addressing.

The Finance Commission makes recommendations on specified fiscal transfers and related matters; the GST Council is a different institution concerned with GST coordination and recommendations. Local governments also need resources and capacity. Transferring funds without usable administrative systems may leave service-delivery gaps.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented divisible pool of 1,000 with a hypothetical states' share of 40% gives 400 to distribute among states. If State A's hypothetical horizontal share is 5%, it receives 20, not 5% of the entire 1,000. These invented percentages are not operative recommendations.

A cess earmarked for a purpose cannot simply be inserted into a divisible-pool calculation as if every Union tax receipt followed the same sharing rule. First identify what enters the pool, then apply vertical and horizontal shares. Grants remain analytically separate from tax devolution.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not confuse devolution with a scheme grant, levy with appropriation, or the Finance Commission with the GST Council. A recommendation, legal provision and actual transfer are different stages.

State borrowing restrictions are not captured by a blanket claim that every borrowing requires Union consent. Relevant constitutional conditions and current rules must be verified before making a legal eligibility statement.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Explain the mismatch in responsibilities and resources, identify the transfer mechanism, then assess equalisation, incentives and autonomy. For local services, connect funding with capacity and accountability. Use current verified recommendations only when the question requires operative percentages; the institutional logic is more durable.

topics.title: Rural credit and microfinance: access with borrower resilience
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Match financing to rural cash flows and compare formal institutions, group finance and borrower-protection risks.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Rural credit finances seasonal production, longer-term investment and household needs in settings where income may be irregular. Working-capital credit pays for inputs and operations; investment credit supports assets such as equipment or land improvement. The timing and purpose of the loan matter as much as its headline interest rate.

Institutional sources include banks and cooperative structures; non-institutional sources include moneylenders and personal networks. Formal access can offer protection and lower costs, but documentation, distance and repayment design may still exclude borrowers. Informal access can be convenient while carrying high costs or weak safeguards.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Farm income often arrives after harvest, while expenditure occurs earlier. A repayment schedule requiring instalments before cash generation can create distress even for a viable activity. Weather, price and health shocks can affect repayment, so credit design must be linked to risk management rather than assuming every sanction improves resilience.

SHG-bank linkage combines group saving and a bank relationship. Joint-liability arrangements use shared responsibility in lending. Microcredit means a loan; microfinance is broader and can involve other services, subject to the provider's legal permissions. Group discipline may reduce information and enforcement problems but does not eliminate household over-indebtedness.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative farmer needs 100 units for inputs and expects sales after six months. A cheaper loan demanding principal in month two may be less suitable than a well-priced loan aligned to harvest. Evaluate repayment capacity, total cost, adequacy and timing together.

A borrower repays one group loan by taking another loan. The repayment rate looks strong while household indebtedness rises. Multiple borrowing and cash-flow assessment therefore matter; repayment pressure is not proof of improved livelihoods or empowerment.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A credit guarantee does not make a loan a grant. More disbursement is not automatically more sustainable income. Not every microfinance institution is legally permitted to accept public deposits, and group sizes or legacy scheme limits are not universal concepts.

Separate seasonal working capital from long-lived asset finance, and access from effective usage and borrower resilience. Do not reproduce an old subsidy or interest rule without its current applicability.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Organise an answer around availability, affordability, adequacy, timeliness and protection. Explain an information or cash-flow constraint, match an institutional response and add safeguards against excessive debt. Combine credit with markets, risk management and productive capability rather than treating lending alone as rural development.

topics.title: Indian taxation: design, GST mechanics and revenue responsiveness
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Compare tax design and compliance mechanisms, apply input-credit logic and interpret revenue responsiveness without relying on stale slabs.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: A tax raises public revenue and changes incentives and distribution. The textbook direct/indirect distinction concerns the legal structure of liability and collection; economic incidence asks who ultimately bears the burden. Legal liability does not prove that the entire economic burden stays with the person who remits the tax.

A progressive tax has a rising average burden relative to income, a proportional tax a constant average burden, and a regressive tax a falling average burden. A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit; an ad valorem tax is based on value. Rate, base and actual collections are separate quantities.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Cascading occurs when tax is imposed on a value that includes earlier tax without an offset. An eligible input-tax credit allows purchase tax to offset output liability, reducing tax-on-tax through the chain. GST credit depends on legal conditions; exemptions, blocked credits and special arrangements prevent treating every input as fully creditable.

The GST Council's recommendations, the GSTN technology interface and tax authorities' administration are distinct. Tax buoyancy measures percentage revenue growth relative to percentage GDP growth, including effects of policy and administration. Tax elasticity aims to isolate responsiveness after relevant discretionary changes are accounted for; buoyancy alone cannot do that separation.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented transaction at an assumed 10% rate: taxable inputs cost 1,000 and output sells for 1,600. Output tax is 160, eligible input credit 100 and net remittance 60. This assumes full eligibility and compatible credit treatment. The 10% is a teaching assumption, not an Indian GST slab.

Invented tax revenue rises from 100 to 115 while nominal GDP rises from 1,000 to 1,100. Revenue grows 15% and GDP 10%, so buoyancy is 1.5. We cannot conclude how much of that response came from automatic growth, rate changes, enforcement or base expansion without further information.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not confuse marginal and average rates, a recommendation and enacted law, tax liability and incidence, or a gross output liability and net remittance after credits. GST does not mean every existing tax disappears.

A higher rate need not always raise collections proportionately because the base, compliance and behaviour can change. That observation does not identify a precise revenue-maximising rate or justify a claim that any rate cut must pay for itself.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Evaluate a tax by revenue adequacy, equity, efficiency, simplicity and compliance. Explain how the base and credit design change incentives, then discuss who bears costs and how revenue is used. Numerical answers should state credit eligibility, valuation and assumptions before calculating.

topics.title: Agriculture: food security, markets and resource trade-offs
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory sector breadth: connect nutrition, price discovery and farm incentives. Deepen scheme eligibility from official current sources; avoid memorising every old subsidy rate.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Agriculture supports food supply, rural livelihoods and inputs for other sectors. Agricultural development is therefore more than maximising one crop's output: productivity, farm income, risk, resource use and access to food must be considered together. A rise in production can coexist with weak earnings if costs rise or realised prices fall.

Food security includes availability, access, utilisation and stability. Grain stocks concern availability; purchasing power and delivery concern access; nutrition, health and diet quality affect utilisation. A country can have adequate aggregate food and still have households unable to obtain a nutritious diet.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Productivity depends on technology, water, soil, knowledge and reliable inputs. Marketing determines how output becomes income: information, transport, storage and competition affect realised prices. Electronic market links can improve information and reach, but cannot alone remove physical logistics or bargaining constraints.

Support policies alter incentives. Cheap power can lower irrigation costs while encouraging excessive groundwater use if extraction is not managed. Price support can reduce some price risk while concentrating gains in crops or regions with stronger procurement access. Assess distribution and ecological effects alongside the intended support.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative farmer harvests more vegetables, but poor storage forces immediate sale when local supply is abundant. Output rose while the realised price fell. Storage, logistics, market information and access to buyers address a different constraint from raising yield.

A district has abundant grain yet persistent child malnutrition. Investigate dietary diversity, household access, sanitation, illness and the reliability of nutrition delivery. More grain production alone need not solve every pathway to poor nutrition.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate production, productivity and farm income. A portal registration is not proof of competitive price discovery. A support price announcement is not proof that all farmers sell at that price.

A food subsidy, farm loan, insurance product and market reform solve different problems. Scheme-era amounts and beneficiary rules require current verification; examples here explain mechanisms rather than endorse operative eligibility.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: For agricultural reform, begin with the constraint: productivity, price risk, market access, credit or sustainability. Explain the instrument's channel, then uneven access and implementation. Conclude with income resilience and nutrition/resource outcomes rather than a target or portal count alone.

topics.title: Industry: reforms, approvals and productive capacity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Study the reform-to-investment channel, not an inventory of launch dates. Distinguish fewer barriers, easier approvals and actual productive investment.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Industrial development expands productive capacity and can support employment, technology and linkages with suppliers. Its contribution depends not only on factory output but also on productivity, working conditions, competitive capability and the ability of smaller firms to participate.

Delicensing reduces specified prior permissions for entry or expansion. Disinvestment changes the government's equity holding. Privatisation involves a transfer into private ownership/control. These instruments address different decisions, so they cannot be used as synonyms.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Firms invest when expected returns justify costs and risks. Simpler approvals can reduce delays, but infrastructure, skills, finance, land access and demand still affect whether investment happens. An information or application portal is a coordination tool, not proof that every approval has been legally granted.

Industrial policy can address coordination failures, technology gaps and infrastructure. It can also create fiscal costs and distort competition if support is poorly targeted or indefinitely protected. Evaluate whether support builds capabilities and whether firms face incentives to become productive rather than depend permanently on assistance.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Illustrative plant receives clearer information about approvals, yet construction stalls because power supply is unreliable and logistics are costly. The approval reform may have reduced one friction without making the whole project viable. Diagnose the remaining bottleneck instead of calling every reform either a complete success or a failure.

If government sells a small shareholding while retaining control, that is disinvestment but not necessarily privatisation. If licensing requirements are reduced, ownership may remain unchanged. The relevant transmission channels are incentives, control and entry barriers, not the labels alone.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: A memorandum of understanding, announced investment, sanctioned project and operating plant are different stages. Production growth is not automatically broad job creation if the activity is highly capital-intensive.
Delicensing is not exemption from labour, environmental, competition or other applicable laws. A single-window interface does not mean every legal authority and safeguard has disappeared.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Build an industrial-policy answer around the bottleneck, the chosen instrument and the intended productivity or employment channel. Add infrastructure, skills and competition conditions, then evaluate realised output, supplier linkages and jobs. Separate announcements and approvals from implementation and outcomes.

topics.title: Services: output, jobs, insurance and logistics
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Cover services through common dimensions: output, employment, productivity, exports and access. Use definitions accurately; update reported sector shares before exam use.

teaching_notes.title: 1. Understand the concept
paragraphs: Services include a wide range of activities, from trade and transport to healthcare, finance and professional work. They differ greatly in skill requirements and productivity. A large services share of GDP therefore does not imply that every worker can immediately obtain a well-paid service job.

Output share measures contribution to production; employment share measures where people work. Labour productivity relates output to workers or hours. A sector can produce a high share of output with fewer workers, while many people remain in lower-productivity activities.

teaching_notes.title: 2. How it works and why it matters
paragraphs: Services can support other sectors: logistics connects producers to markets, finance mobilises resources, and communication reduces coordination costs. Weak services can raise costs throughout the economy. Development requires the supporting infrastructure and skills, not merely a new platform or headline growth rate.

Insurance penetration is premiums relative to GDP; insurance density is premiums per person. They measure different denominators. Neither directly measures adequate coverage, claim settlement or financial protection for vulnerable households. Increased premium payments can coexist with gaps in usable protection.

teaching_notes.title: 3. Worked example
paragraphs: Invented premiums 40, GDP 1,000 and population 20 give penetration of 4% and density of 2 currency units per person. Density is not a percentage. These are mathematical illustrations, not actual insurance indicators.

A highly productive digital service expands output but recruits only specialised workers. Its growth may be valuable without absorbing all displaced low-skill workers. Skill development and a broader range of labour-absorbing activities are needed to connect output growth with inclusive employment.

teaching_notes.title: 4. Distinctions and exam traps
paragraphs: Do not equate a high output share with an equal employment share or use penetration and density interchangeably. Insurance sales are not proof that customers understand exclusions or can obtain adequate claims.
A logistics target is not an achieved cost reduction. Compare consistent coverage, units and reference periods before repeating a claim about India's service or insurance performance.

teaching_notes.title: 5. Building an analytical answer
paragraphs: Explain the service's direct contribution and its linkages with other sectors. Distinguish high-productivity segments from broad employment opportunities, then address skills and access.
